blocks.text: This small parish lies between the parishes of São Jorge and Boaventura. It is about six kilometres from the parish church of São Jorge and approximately two from that of Boaventura.

The shape of the surrounding hills amply explains its name. It belonged to the parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge from that parish’s creation in 1517 until it separated from it in 1676. It naturally took the name Arco de São Jorge, which long predates the parish’s creation.

Pedro Gomes Galdo was one of Madeira’s earliest settlers. He received extensive lands under *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in São Jorge and Boaventura, and we presume these included the lands that later formed the parish of Arco de São Jorge. We cannot know when settlement began in Arco or when its lands were first cleared for cultivation. It seems to us, however, that this happened towards the end of the 15th century or in the first quarter of the 16th, well before the parish of São Jorge was created.

A small chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) once stood on the spot now occupied by the locality (*sítio*) of Casais. The year of its foundation is unknown, but we presume it dates from the third or last quarter of the 16th century. It had its own chaplain, who conducted services there under the authority of the vicar of São Jorge. This chapel became the seat of the new parish, established by the diocesan prelate Dom António Teles da Silva under the authority granted by the royal decree (alvará régio) of Peter II dated 28 December 1676.

Long before the parish was created, the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade was already in a lamentable state of repair and threatened with imminent ruin. Only ten years after it became the parish seat, Bishop Dom Estêvão Brioso de Figueiredo visited it in person. Finding the small chapel too cramped and unsuitable as a parish church, he ordered that an application be made for the immediate construction of a new church. It was not until half a century later, by order of the Treasury Council dated 18 January 1740, that construction of the new church was authorised. It was blessed on 19 March 1744 by the vicar at the time, Father Manuel da Costa.

We know that Fathers João Batista and José de Andrade served as chaplains of the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade before the parish was created. The latter was the first priest to serve there as parish priest. He was succeeded in the care of souls by Fathers Francisco da Costa, Francisco Manuel Pereira, Bartolomeu Marques Caldeira, Joaquim Baptista Catanho, Bernardo Ribeiro, etc.

blocks.text: This small parish is perhaps the most fertile on the whole of Madeira’s north coast. It produces every kind of crop, and its land is particularly well suited to growing sugar cane. Its output would be greater, however, if irrigation water were not scarce. A considerable part of its land grows only cereals and vegetables, and even these crops depend on rainfall. To remedy this, a levada (irrigation channel) must be built. Beginning at the locality of Falca in the parish of Boaventura, it would irrigate many fields in that parish and in Arco de São Jorge. Surveys and plans were completed more than thirty years ago, when the works were estimated to cost about thirty *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis). During the 1890 legislative session, the deputy Canon Feliciano João Teixeira advocated this important improvement before the national assembly. Work on the levada was never begun, however, and it remained only a proposal.

The fertility of this parish’s soil is matched by its healthy conditions and mild climate. Mortality is low, and some epidemics that have struck Madeira, such as the cholera outbreak of 1856, have not reached it. Its climate is among the mildest and most temperate on the whole north coast. High mountains shelter the settlement from the harsh, biting winds of winter. This does not, however, prevent common illnesses or even epidemic diseases from appearing here, as they do everywhere. We know that an epidemic illness claimed many lives here in 1768. On that occasion, António Rodrigues Seabra, the surgeon of the parish of Boaventura, rendered valuable service, while the parish church’s funds provided substantial donations to combat the epidemic. Another illness appeared in this parish in 1849. Classified at the time as diarrhoea, it affected countless people and claimed many lives. The district’s civil governor, the public-spirited Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, went there in person, accompanied by two doctors and the supplies needed to treat the sick. The illness died out soon afterwards. (See *Epocha Administrativa*, vol. 2, p. 506 ff.).

The principal localities of this parish are Igreja, Casais, Lagoa, Poços, Arco Pequeno and Quebrada. The last owes its name to the great landslide (*quebrada*) that fell there more than two centuries ago. Large areas of land broke away, chiefly from Arco Pequeno, forming that locality. Such events are common in Madeira: the parish of Jardim do Mar, part of the parish of Paul, the locality of Lugar de Baixo and others were formed in the same way. The landslide at Arco de São Jorge had, however, a remarkable feature deserving special mention. We have found several references to it, including in Dr Pereira Drumond’s *Noticias Mineralogicas da Ilha da Madeira*, published in 1818 in the *Investigador Portuguez*, and in other Portuguese and foreign authors. These accounts agree closely with local tradition, which still preserves the story intact. Interesting details of this extraordinary event appear in a letter discovered in 1848 at the Public Library of Lisbon (*Biblioteca Pública de Lisboa*) by General Antonio Pedro de Azevedo. Some years ago, a Funchal newspaper published the remarkable extract reproduced below (see *Verdade*, no. 944): ‘I give Your Grace this news because it is a marvellous occurrence. On the far side of the island, at Arco de São Jorge, where most of the land is an estate belonging to my entail (*morgado*), the ground had for many years been split by a great fissure. The land is very steep, and after this year’s severe winter weather, at about midnight on Easter Day, a great mass of earth moved out into the sea for about half a *légua*, carrying the rocks and shoals before it so gently that the houses, trees and vine trellises remained standing. In one house, two barrels of wine stood on the supports of the canteiro system (natural ageing of the wine in casks on wooden supports, without artificial heating) without overturning. A beehive on a slab of stone did not fall, and a brooding hen with eggs, tethered beside a fig tree, was found there too. Everything remained in place, and the ground was undisturbed. It formed an island in the sea with land enough to sow about twenty *moios*. The land is continuing to join up with it. A beach formed, with two fine harbours that this part of the coast needed, for its shoals had made it impossible to load anything aboard a boat there. Where the earth moved from, a deep hollow was left above, bounded by a sheer cliff; below lies an excellent *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff) of new land, extending to meet the land in the sea. Before, there had been a very high cliff where the land met the sea. It moved without a crash and without anyone noticing, except for one man who saw it moving at night and suffered a seizure. It was like a boat being launched into the sea, running along its slipway. The wonder is that, for three days beforehand, across the width of the land that moved, the tide neither rose nor fell at all. The sea there seemed dead, while on either side it ebbed and flowed with the usual waves of the north coast.’
This happened in 1689. If it occurred on Easter Sunday, as the letter states, it must have been on 20 April of that year.

blocks.text: The most distinguished son of this parish was Antonio Gil Gomes, whom we shall discuss more fully in the appropriate entry. Antonio Januario Moderno was also born there, on 25 February 1789, the son of Captain João Rodrigues Moderno and Dona Antonia da Incarnação Moderno. He was superintendent of Machico, whose jurisdiction then included the municipality (*concelho*) of Sant’Ana, and held other public offices. He was celebrated throughout the island in his day, not only for the spirited hospitality with which he received guests at his home in Arco, but above all for his Herculean strength. His many remarkable feats of daring made him both feared and respected. In London, where he lived as a political exile, he also became known among his compatriots for his courage and the strength of his arm. He died in Funchal on 11 October 1864. His son, Dr Antonio Januario Moderno, graduated in medicine from a foreign university and practised with great success and skill in the United States, where he amassed a large fortune. He too was born in the parish of Arco de São Jorge. He spent almost his entire life outside Madeira, but died in this city about thirty years ago, shortly after returning to his native land. He had earned a reputation as a man of exceptional talent and an accomplished physician. He died in Funchal on 11 February 1885, aged 67.

The distinguished priest Antonio Alexandrino de Vasconcelos was born in the parish of Boaventura in 1791. He lived in Arco de São Jorge for more than forty consecutive years and died there in 1884. He served as vicar general of the bishopric and held other important posts. In 1834 he accompanied the prelate Dom Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade when the latter was forced into exile and went to Italy. He was a cleric of remarkable intelligence and learning, regarded as a leading authority on the various branches of Catholic liturgy.

The patron saint of this parish was Nossa Senhora da Piedade until 1744, when the new church was built and St Joseph became its patron. Papal briefs of 24 and 26 August 1784 designated the altar in the chancel a privileged altar and granted a plenary indulgence to be gained on St Joseph’s feast day. We found, somewhere, the curious information that Francisco Aurélio da Câmara Leme, holder of an entail, charged his statutory share of his estate with a perpetual obligation to supply the oil needed to light the Blessed Sacrament in the church of Arco de São Jorge. His son and heir, Francisco Antonio da Câmara Leme, who also held the entail, confirmed and assumed this obligation by a public deed dated 18 February 1766. The charge fell on ‘the *quinta* (country estate) opposite Santo Amaro’.

Until just a few years ago, Arco de São Jorge had the lowest rate of illiteracy among the island’s rural parishes outside municipal centres. Illiteracy, as we know, is so deeply and regrettably entrenched here in Madeira. This distinction was due to the diligence with which some parish priests provided primary education there. Father Isilio Joaquim Vares deserves particular mention for his work in the second quarter of the 19th century, as do the later priests Father Emilio Marques da Silva, Father Francisco Manuel de Sousa, Father Francisco Antonio de Abreu and Father Casimiro Augusto de Freitas. On 16 January 1886, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Sant’Ana established a state school for boys in Arco de São Jorge, which has provided valuable service there. Some years later it became a mixed school.

This parish belongs to the municipality of Sant’Ana and the judicial district (*comarca*) of São Vicente. It lies approximately twelve and a half kilometres from both their administrative centres, about forty-one kilometres from Funchal by the Poiso road and thirty-seven by way of Curral das Freiras and Boaventura. Its population is 167 inhabitants. We should also mention that the celebrated popular poet Manuel Gonçalves was born in this parish. Known as Manuel Feiticeiro, he died a few years ago. He travelled throughout the island singing his artless verse, much to the delight of the crowds who listened to him avidly and bought the dozens of pamphlets in which he collected and had printed his many imperfectly written songs.
See Popular Poetry.

blocks.text: The sugar industry flourished here in Madeira from the 15th to the 17th century, despite the burdensome restrictions and extremely heavy taxes imposed on it. Madeiran sugar was then known in the principal European markets. Captain Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, well known for his generosity, once sent Pope Leo X several valuable gifts, notably a representation of the Sacred College made from sugar, with life-sized cardinals fashioned entirely from *alfenim* (white sugar paste for modelling figures).

In the early days, sugar cane was pressed in alçapremas (hand-operated lever presses) or in very rudimentary sugar mills (*engenhos*). The mills’ rollers were sometimes made from thick trunks of til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), suitably prepared.

In 1496, there was sugar boiled once and sugar boiled twice. The latter cost 600 réis and the former 350 réis per *arroba* (a weight of about 15 kg). Before that, each *arroba* of sugar cost 339 réis, probably for the second grade.
The owner of a sugar mill gave Prince Henry the Navigator, Lord of the Island, a third of the sugar produced. The owner of an alçaprema gave only one and a half *arrobas* of sugar each month.
Shortly after 1452, Funchal had only one water-powered sugar mill, while alçapremas were numerous because the tax imposed on them was less onerous.
The original charter (*foral*), perhaps granted by Afonso V, required sugar mills to surrender a third of their output and also required half of any cane not made into sugar to be handed over.

Over time, the area under sugar cane expanded as levadas (irrigation channels) were built to water the land. Meanwhile, the levy on sugar mills fell to a quarter and then a fifth (*quintos*, a levy of one fifth on sugar) of their sugar. As a result, the number of mills grew. Together with the alçapremas, they produced more than 120,000 *arrobas* of sugar around 1498 and more than 300,000 *arrobas* by the middle of the 16th century.
This sugar was consumed in Madeira, in Portugal and in many foreign countries. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 26 August 1503 ended the restrictions previously imposed on its export.

The royal decree of 22 March 1498 allowed foreigners to reside permanently on the island, a right denied them by the regulations (*regimento*) of 7 October 1496. The charter of 21 January 1511 then allowed those same foreigners to ship sugar for export.
This sugar had to be cleared through customs houses. From 1512 onwards, clearance took place solely at the Funchal customs house.

In 1507, sugar cost 315 réis per *arroba*, and in 1511 it cost 300 réis. The influx of sugar from Brazil and the Spanish colonies in the Americas into European markets was the main cause of Madeira’s sugar industry decline. Madeira was still exporting some sugar in 1612, but by 1649 many of its sugar mills lay in ruins, and few remained in 1730.
In 1736, Madeira began importing sugar from abroad. It continued to do so, on a greater or lesser scale, until sugar cultivation was re-established after *Oidium Tuckery* destroyed the vineyards.

Between 1823 and 1826, Madeira produced an insignificant quantity of sugar. By 1861, output was 275,802 kilograms, rising to between 800,000 and 900,000 kilograms a year from 1870 to 1873. In more recent years, sugar was produced in the following quantities:

These figures do not include the colonial sugar imported by the island. Local consumption amounted to 1,102,545 kilograms of sugar in 1908, 837,500 in 1912 and 1,656,310 kilograms in 1916, with surplus production exported to Portugal. In 1938, local consumption was 3,069,143 kilograms, while 399,780 kilograms were exported to the mainland.

According to Dr Azevedo, exports of Madeiran sugar in modern times began in 1854. They grew rapidly from 1858, reaching their peak in 1871 and 1872: 561,837 kilograms in the first year and 567,526 kilograms in the second. They then fell by half in 1873 and declined further and further until 1881. The early manufacturers said that 100 kilograms of Bourbon cane, an exceptionally rich variety, yielded around 7 to 9 kilograms of sugar, despite the very rudimentary production methods used. Today, it is known that the average sugar yield of Yuba cane varies between 9 and 101 per cent, a fact attributable mainly to improvements in production methods.

blocks.text: Under Madeira’s sugar regime (*regime sacarino*, the legal framework governing sugar production), the price of sugar is set according to the price of sugar cane. First-quality sugar, sold for 29 centavos in 1914, rose to 31 centavos the following year and then continued to rise until it reached 36 centavos per kilogram. In 1900, it sold for 26.5 to 27.5 centavos; many years earlier, its price had ranged from 20 to 24 centavos per kilogram. In 1939, it costs 4.20 escudos at the factory and 4.40 escudos at retail.

Second-quality sugar, sold for 24 and 25 centavos per kilogram in 1910, cost 28 centavos in 1914, then rose to 30 and finally 33 centavos. Before the war, this sugar was sold to refineries in Lisbon for 18 and 19 centavos per kilogram.

Sugar is made at the Torreão Factory. Decree no. 23,847 of 14 May 1934, referring to decree no. 16,003 of 29 October 1928, stipulates that until 1953, or until increased consumption justifies a change, no new sugar or alcohol factories may be built. Nor may the existing factory’s production capacity be increased, or a factory that only distils be adapted to make sugar. All may, however, make the machinery improvements necessary under the law.

Since 1935, sugar production has in principle been limited to local consumption. This limit, combined with the obligation to buy all sugar cane meeting a specified grade, means that the current regime guarantees the industry the Madeira market. If there is a surplus in any production year, up to 200 tonnes of sugar may be sent to mainland Portugal duty-free. Larger exports have, however, already been permitted exceptionally for specific reasons concerning the interests of agriculture and industry.
See Spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), Alcohol, Sugar Cane and Sugar Protectionism.

João Gonçalves Zarco was a Homeric figure at the dawn of our maritime ventures and voyages. He led the most important discovery made by Portuguese seamen in the first quarter of the 15th century, under the fruitful and glorious guidance of the Great Infante, Henry the Navigator. The discovery of Madeira is the great, enduring commemorative pillar (padrão) that marks the auspicious beginning of our odyssey as navigators. It represents not only a remarkable expansion of our nation’s territory but, above all, our first great achievement as navigators and future masters of the seas.

The name of the illustrious navigator is inseparably linked to this momentous event in our history. The influence of this great discovery on our subsequent maritime ventures has not been given due prominence. Yet there can be no doubt that it was exceptionally important: the discoverer and first coloniser of Madeira deserves a prominent place in the finest pages of our maritime chronicles.

Gonçalo Velho Cabral, who discovered the islands of São Miguel and Santa Maria, has won greater renown in history. A distinguished biographer gave a detailed account of him as a navigator, drawing on extensive historical research and showing the painstaking care with which a descendant proud of his ancestral lineage celebrates his forebears’ exploits. João Gonçalves Zarco had no descendant to write his biography, nor has anyone researched him in the public archives beyond what Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo found in the documents held by this city’s municipal registry. The result is a striking lack of accounts and information about the great navigator. It is extremely difficult even to attempt a brief biography that sketches, in broad outline, his most distinctive qualities as a warrior, navigator and coloniser (1921).

Zarco or Zargo? Frutuoso’s learned commentator, himself a distinguished philologist, answers that Zarco is the more authentic spelling of this surname and is supported by the most reputable authors, but that it became antiquated and usage adopted Zargo. We have consulted the earliest chroniclers and writers who dealt, however briefly, with the discoverer of our archipelago, including Gomes Eanes de Zurara, João de Barros and Damião de Góis. We found that all wrote Zarco, and that the accounts of voyages made by Diogo Gomes, a contemporary of Prince Henry the Navigator, and by Alvise Cadamosto (1450) use the same spelling. A royal letter (*carta régia*) from Afonso V, dated 1449, has the much older form Zarquo, corresponding to the Zarco used by our early chroniclers. The renowned historian of the islands, who wrote his work in the last quarter of the 16th century, uses the modernised form Zargo. The spelling Zarco, found in two or three places in the *Saudades*, should be regarded as a copyist’s slip or a printing error, since Gaspar Frutuoso writes Zargo many dozens, perhaps hundreds, of times. The annotator of that work also invariably adopted this spelling. Every consideration favours using today the spelling employed by the illustrious author of *Saudades da Terra* and his learned commentator.

What is the origin of the surname Zarco or Zargo, used by the illustrious discoverer of Madeira? João de Barros and, after him, Damião de Góis – followed in turn by Gaspar Frutuoso, the chronicler of the islands – said that Zarco or Zargo was a nickname arising from a heroic deed performed by the navigator, not a surname inherited from his noble ancestors. The learned annotator of the *Saudades* disagrees with those chroniclers. He says that the versions Frutuoso gives cannot be accepted as true: they are simply another example of the usual way legends are invented, by attaching an unknown name to a person and breaking it down into a more or less plausible fable. In support of his assertion, he cites several old genealogies in which the discoverer’s forebears bear the surname Zarco or Zargo.

It will not be entirely out of place to recount here, though very briefly, the versions given by Gaspar Frutuoso that we mentioned above. During one of our engagements in Morocco, a Moor who was a bold and skilful horseman challenged a Portuguese warrior to a fierce fight. The Portuguese warrior was defeated, though he paid for his exceptional courage with his life. Another Portuguese horseman, and apparently several more, took up the relentless fight. All met the same unhappy fate, until the captain of our stronghold refused to allow any more lives to be sacrificed to the ferocious fury of the fearsome Moor. Then a horseman who had not yet distinguished himself by his courage appeared and pleaded insistently for permission to charge the victorious Moor. Let us now hear the author of the *Saudades* in his artless, picturesque words: ‘And at once the soldier asked for the horse of a knight whom he had chosen for the purpose. Mounting it with a shield on his arm and a piece of wood in his other hand, he rode towards the Moor, who, seeing him manoeuvre, came at him with great arrogance. Each time the Moor tried to strike the Christian, the latter did no more than turn aside his lance. He continued thus until, seeing his moment, he charged the Moor swiftly on horseback and dealt him such a great blow where he was unprotected that he stunned him, seized him by the hair and delivered him as a prisoner to the captain. By this deed he became known to the king. Some say that João Gonçalves Zargo was descended from this valiant soldier, as his son or grandson; others say that João Gonçalves himself performed this feat of arms. And because the Moor whom he, or his father, or his grandfather killed was called Zargo, they, or he, took the same surname and name.’

Our first conquest in Africa took place in 1415, and Madeira was discovered four or five years later. It is hard to believe that the discoverer’s grandfather, surely already well advanced in years by then, could have been the hero of that exploit. It would be more plausible to attribute it to his father, and more plausible still to the navigator himself. But the chronicler himself seems to have placed little faith in the story, for he adds: ‘The account I have from the island of Madeira tells of this beginning differently:...’ He goes on to say that at the siege of Tangier, ‘Zargo proved himself so fine a knight, showing such great courage as he fought valiantly before the Infantes, that they held him in high esteem. In that place and in the fighting, he was struck in one eye by a crossbow bolt shot by the enemy, which destroyed the eye. Since at that time a man with only one eye was called *zargo*, the name remained with him as a badge and honour of his knighthood. For he showed such prowess and distinguished himself so greatly as a knight that his courage and skill in the war contributed in no small measure to Prince Henry’s escape to the sea, just as Infante Ferdinand was being taken captive through treachery and cunning, as is recounted at length in the *Chronica d’El-Rey D. Duarte*’.

Friar Francisco Brandão says in *Monarchia Lusitana*: ‘There is no reason to accept the explanation that Dr Gaspar Frutuoso gives in his history of the islands, saying that.... Zarco was a nickname because he was blind in one eye or because he had killed a Moor in Africa named Zarco....’

Also concerning the origin of the discoverer’s surname, one of the notes to *Saudades* reproduces the following passage from a genealogical work by José Freire Monterroio Mascarenhas: ‘The Zarco family is almost as old as the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), for records of it have been found in its archives dating back to the 12th century. Although we know that there is a *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) in the province of Alentejo, near the town (*vila*) of Viana do Alentejo, named Zarco, it has always seemed to us that the family did not take its surname from there. Rather, the surname came not from a manor house but from a nickname: in both Castilian and Portuguese, the word *Zarco* means a man with greenish eyes. António de Nebrixa translates it in his *Diccionário* by the Latin word *glaucus*, as do Jerónimo Cardoso in his *Vocabulário* and Ambrósio Calepino in his *Diccionario*. It was thus given to one person as a nickname and passed from that person to their descendants as a surname’.

flags.note: The quoted title Chronica d'El-Rey D. Duarte retains its original spelling; the personal reference to Infante D. Henrique is rendered Prince Henry.
Modernised the spellings of António de Nebrixa, Jerónimo Cardoso and Ambrósio Calepino without name-table entries.

blocks.text: We do not know where João Gonçalves Zargo was born. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says ‘the authors disagree about his birthplace: some hold that he was a native of Tomar because the Zarco family had an estate there, as the chronicler Brandão says; others say Lisbon; and some say Matosinhos or Porto, where Lousada says the Zarcos had a chapel.’

Some early Madeiran genealogies give Matosinhos as Zargo’s birthplace, and the writer Francisco Manuel de Melo, a descendant of the discoverer, also states that he was born there. The third captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the discoverer’s grandson, left his captaincy and settled in Matosinhos, where he died in 1530 (volume I, page 207). It has been conjectured that he moved to this part of mainland Portugal because his family may have come from there, retained family traditions there or owned property in the village. None of these reasons conclusively proves that the great navigator was born in Matosinhos, but they are certainly grounds for considering the claim carefully. We should add that we were recently assured that the locality still has a tradition that the discoverer of this archipelago was born there.

What was his exact date of birth? One of the annotations to Frutuoso’s work reads: ‘We do not know precisely in which years João Gonçalves Zarco lived. Since he was a young man in 1419, and since his eldest son, João Gonçalves da Câmara, died aged eighty-seven in . . . March 1501 and was therefore born in 1414, we infer that Zargo was born around 1395.’ It seems to us that Zargo’s birth should be placed shortly after 1390, making him between 25 and 30 at the time of the discovery. Some chroniclers describe him then as a young man, still not far advanced in years. We must not forget, however, that he had already distinguished himself as a navigator and had behaved heroically during the second siege of Ceuta.

If we credit the genealogist Freire Mascarenhas, cited above, João Gonçalves Zarco was the son of Gonçalo Esteves Zarco and Dona Brites. She was the daughter of João Afonso of Santarém, an overseer in the household of King John I. Gonçalo Esteves, who lived during the reigns of Afonso IV, Peter I and Ferdinand, was the son of Estevão Pires Zarco, who was said to be an advocate in the King’s household and held important judicial posts.

The navigator Gonçalves Zargo’s name gains no greater glory from his distinguished ancestors or his membership of a family with noble traditions, though such things were of paramount importance at the time. Nevertheless, truth requires us to say that the discoverer of the archipelago came from noble stock and, as such, was a member of Prince Henry’s household. The old chroniclers Eanes de Azurara and João de Barros say so; the historian of the islands confirms it; and the same account appears in the oldest and most respected Madeiran genealogies. A genealogy of Zargo in a nobiliary by José Freire Monterroio de Mascarenhas, already cited above, traces the illustrious navigator’s known ancestors back to the 12th century. Its manuscript is held in the Lisbon Public Library. In our view, one of the strongest proofs of his noble origins is his marriage to Dona Constança Rodrigues de Sá. She was the daughter of Rodrigo Aires de Sá, who represented Portugal in Rome and there married Dona Cecília Colona, daughter of the Marquis and Prince of Colona, whose family was among the oldest, noblest and most esteemed of the Roman patriciate. This has recently been confirmed to us by a distinguished researcher from mainland Portugal, following several searches of old and authoritative documents (1921). It is worth noting that a marriage contracted under such circumstances at that time, when Zargo had not yet won renown as a celebrated discoverer or become the wealthy captain-donatary of Funchal, could only have taken place if the bridegroom had standing and proven noble ancestry. Aires de Sá, who misses no opportunity to praise the discoverer of the Azores in extravagant terms and sometimes refers to the discoverer of Madeira with manifest unfairness, says that João Gonçalves Zargo ‘was a man of modest origins . . . who managed to rise in Prince Henry’s household and went on to become a settler’. But the truth is that he offers no evidence for his assertion, which directly contradicts what the chroniclers, the genealogies and the customs of the time tell us.

blocks.text: The genealogist Freire Monterroio, cited above, says that Gonçalves Zargo began ‘serving Prince Henry the Navigator when he was very young’. He therefore had a long apprenticeship under that illustrious and worthy prince. Zargo distinguished himself as a navigator, making several voyages along the African coast. At the time, this was the proven training ground, the arduous course through which our daring seamen gained experience. Some writers, among them Francisco Manuel de Melo, claim that the illustrious navigator was the first to introduce firearms aboard his ships. They thus credit his inventive genius and martial zeal with this advance in warfare at sea. He served as captain of the Algarve coast and fought several engagements at sea against Moors and Castilians, always showing exceptional courage.

The discoverer of Madeira also distinguished himself as a brave and daring soldier. The chronicles give highly favourable accounts of his heroic conduct at Ceuta and Tangier. At Ceuta he was knighted. During the disastrous action at Tangier, he did much to ensure that Prince Henry the Navigator could embark under protection from Moorish attacks. Frutuoso says of this: ‘Through the skill and courage of this knight João Gonçalves Zargo, Prince Henry the Navigator withdrew and embarked on the ships waiting at sea for that purpose. Zargo remained ashore throughout, gathering as many of the men as he could and bravely withstanding the onslaught and weight of the Moors, who came against him to prevent the Prince from boarding. After the men had withdrawn, with the loss of many Portuguese, João Gonçalves himself withdrew, badly wounded, with difficulty and in danger, for the Moors were countless. For this great service that the magnanimous João Gonçalves Zargo rendered the Prince, and for others he had rendered the King, they held him in high esteem. The King gave him important offices, in which he always proved himself a worthy knight.’ His descendants continued his glorious example. Many of them, especially his successors in the captaincy, distinguished themselves by their valour in the African strongholds, as we have already noted in the articles devoted to them in the first volume of this work (1921).

Shortly after the discovery of this archipelago and the division of its captaincies, Gonçalves Zargo settled in Funchal with his wife and children and began settling and colonising his donatary captaincy (*donataria*). ‘Captain João Gonçalves Zargo,’ says *Saudades da Terra*, ‘sheltered his ships by the islets at the cape of this place, where there was a fine cove. He resolved to build himself a wooden dwelling on land and promptly built it beside the sea, on high ground where the captain’s wife (*capitoa*, wife of the captain-donatary), Constança Rodrigues, later founded a church of Santa Catarina.’ Beside this small church stood Zargo’s first residence. It was doubtless a more than modest and uncomfortable wooden house, with a single floor and no architectural ornament, like all the earliest houses built here in Madeira.

We have said elsewhere that it was in the secluded retreat of Santa Catarina that Zargo directed the first work of colonisation and laid the foundations of the future town (*vila*). It advanced rapidly and achieved remarkable growth within his lifetime. Perhaps there he dreamt of the progress of the captaincy of which he was donatary (*donatário*), and of the rise of the family he had founded. He may have foreseen the honours and privileges that his descendants and successors would soon receive. Perhaps he even guessed that the monarch would reward him with the insignia of nobility and the right to bear a coat of arms. He might already have pictured the documents recording his grandsons’ titles adorned with the coronets of counts and grandees of the Kingdom, in tribute to their grandfather’s services...

Some years later, the discoverer moved his residence to the left bank of the stream, at the foot of the hill later called Pico dos Frias. It stood near the chapel he had built there with a dedication to São Paulo. This is said to have been the first stone dwelling house built in Funchal.

His final home, where he spent most of his life, stood very near the site on which he had the church of Conceição de Cima built. An old manuscript says: ‘He also resolved to make a dwelling for himself, as he did on a height above the Funchal valley, directly opposite a church of Nossa Senhora da Conceição, to serve as a family vault for himself and his kin.’ That church is now the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), while his residence is the old manor house of the Lomelino entailed-estate holders, known today as Quinta das Cruzes. The reader may find a fuller account in the article ‘Moradias de Zargo’, on page 395 of volume II of this work, to which we refer them.

We know that João Gonçalves Zarco worked tirelessly to colonise his captaincy. Its seat rapidly grew in importance and was raised to the status of a town a quarter of a century after settlement began, while the discoverer was still alive. About fifty years later, it was granted city status by a royal decree (alvará régio) of 21 August 1508. Few details are known of the first donatary’s government, but nothing is known that reflects badly on the public administration of his captaincy. One accusation has been made against him: that he started the voracious fire which destroyed a considerable part of the vigorous woodland that originally covered the island from the ocean’s edge to the mountain summits. This event, recounted at some length on page 140 of volume 2 of the *Elucidário*, was certainly a reckless undertaking. The first settlers may not have been able to judge its disastrous consequences. Yet rapid, extensive colonisation also made it imperative to clear some of those dense, impenetrable thickets. Only a fire could reduce them sufficiently to allow farming to begin at once. According to João de Barros, the fire appears to have caused serious damage and difficulties for the early settlement because it spread over such a large area. It is also beyond doubt that Madeira’s forests regenerated rapidly and that the island was soon covered in abundant vegetation. The letter of grant (carta de doação) by which Prince Henry the Navigator gave João Gonçalves Zarco the captaincy of Funchal dates from 1 November 1450. Under that same letter, the captaincy would pass to his direct successors. The Prince’s letter was confirmed by royal letters of 25 November 1451 and 16 August 1461. The privileges and rights conferred by these documents were essentially the same as those set out in the letters of grant made to the donataries Tristão Vaz Teixeira and Bartolomeu Perestrelo. The donataries’ powers were exceedingly broad and even highly discretionary: they held all civil and criminal jurisdiction, except the power to impose the death penalty or the cutting off of a limb. They were masters of water and wind, meaning that only they could own mills, whether windmills or watermills. They also held the exclusive rights to make bread and sell salt. In addition, they received a tenth of the revenues assigned to the Prince and held the important prerogative of distributing uncultivated land. Together, these rights brought the captains-donatary of Funchal a very substantial annual income, making the household of this captaincy’s donataries one of the wealthiest in the country. Zarco’s fourth-generation descendant, the 5th donatary, was made Count of Calheta and a grandee of the realm. The donataries of Funchal built a palace as their residence in Lisbon and lived in great splendour in the capital. We know of no land or other real property on this island that Gonçalves Zarco reserved for himself or his successors in the donatary captaincy. We do know, however, that he granted vast territories to his other children and sons-in-law, including Lombada in Ponta do Sol (volume II, page 277), as well as others.

Of Madeira’s first donataries, Zarco enjoyed the greatest prestige and influence. This was surely due to his personal qualities, not merely to his being ‘a person of higher standing than Tristão Vaz’, as Barros says in his first *Década*. The choice of captaincy already seems to suggest the superiority accorded to Funchal’s donatary. The seat of his donatary captaincy had an admirable location, ample space for a large settlement, a spacious harbour, fertile soil, picturesque surroundings and a mild climate. By comparison, Madeira’s other captaincy was plainly inferior in its terrain and climate, its lack of beaches and landing places, the difficulty of communications, etc. These differences leave no doubt about the preference given to Gonçalves Zarco when the land discovered by the two navigators was divided. Later, as Funchal developed rapidly and remarkably, its donataries’ influence continued to grow. At times they abused it by extending their jurisdiction into the other donatary captaincies, plainly encroaching on others’ powers. The disastrous administration of the captains-donatary of Machico and Porto Santo contributed considerably to this. To some extent, the governments of mainland Portugal sanctioned the practice: they did not curb the abuses and, in official documents, called Funchal’s donatary ‘the captain of the island’, as though the captaincy of Machico did not exist.

As noted above, João Gonçalves Zargo married Constança Rodrigues de Sá, also called Constança Rodrigues de Almeida. According to the most authoritative genealogists, she was the daughter of Rodrigo Aires de Sá, Portugal’s ambassador in Rome, and Cecília Colona, of the highly distinguished Roman family of the Marquises of Colona. A genealogical article says of that family: ‘A Roman patrician family whose origins go back to Pietro de Colona, lord of a castle near Rome, who lived around 1100. His great-great-great-grandson Seiarra de Colona was made a marquis in 1289. His descendants were later made Princes of Colona and Palestrina and Grandees of Spain; theirs is one of the most ancient lineages among Italian families....’ On the balance of probability, and according to the genealogies we have been able to consult, the discoverer of our archipelago brought his wife Constança Rodrigues de Sá, their eldest son João Gonçalves da Câmara and their daughter Helena Gonçalves da Câmara with him when he came to begin colonisation. Their third child, Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, the 3rd captain-donatary of the island of São Miguel, was very probably born in Madeira. We have already dealt, albeit briefly, with the discoverer’s earliest descendants in the article *Filhos e Genros de Zargo* (volume II, page 31), to which we refer our readers. We must, however, correct what we said there about Garcia Gonçalves da Câmara: he was the legitimate son of João Gonçalves Zargo and Constança Rodrigues, not the illustrious navigator’s son born outside marriage. We took that information from a less authoritative source which we then believed reliable. In the article *Donatários*, we described the immediate succession of Funchal’s captains-donatary, direct descendants of the discoverer until the period of Philippine rule. We also devoted a separate, fairly detailed article to each of them on pages 201 and following of volume I of this work.

Zargo had numerous distinguished descendants, who spread across Madeira, the Azores, Brazil and mainland Portugal. Some became the founders of illustrious titled houses. One of his descendants, the great writer Francisco Manuel de Melo, says:

‘.... João Gonçalves Zarco, a man renowned among us: setting aside the older houses, which are too uncertain to record, few men in Portugal have had such abundant descendants. Three counts bearing this surname – those of Calheta, Vila Franca and Atouguia – trace their male line to him..... And through marriage, 21 holders of titles in this kingdom descend from João Gonçalves’. By a document dated 4 July 1460, Afonso V granted the illustrious discoverer the right to use a coat of arms, described in the document as follows: ‘a black shield, and at its foot a green mountain on which stands a silver tower between two golden wolves...’. In this royal letter the discoverer is named João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos, the name his successors were supposed to use. In fact, they do not appear to have done so, nor does Zargo himself. We have already said enough about his coat of arms, the historical error it contains, the surname Câmara used by his descendants, etc., in the article *Câmara*, on page 198 of volume I of this *Elucidário*.

blocks.text: Gonçalves Zargo died at a very advanced age. An old manuscript gives a vivid account: ‘He lived to such an age that men carried him in their arms to watch the sunset, which greatly strengthened him. From there he directed matters within his jurisdiction, governing and administering justice with his faculties intact, never showing the mental weakness of a decrepit man.’ Some old genealogical works give 1451 as the year of the navigator’s death, others 1461 and another 1471. Nothing definite is known. The year 1451 cannot be accepted, because a royal letter dated 4 July 1460 shows that Zargo was still alive that year. The date 1461, considered the most likely, agrees best with the 40 years of administration of the captaincy attributed to him by the historian of the islands. On the other hand, if we accept that he was born between 1390 and 1395, as we said above, he would have been between 66 and 71 when he died. That hardly accords with the great age described by the chroniclers, especially in that era. If we accept 1471 as the year of his death and 1390 as the year of his birth, he would have reached 81, fully justifying the chroniclers’ unanimous account of his decrepitude. He may, however, have been born before 1390, in which case the dates 1451 and 1461 might also be justified. These are mere conjectures: we do not yet have evidence that would allow us to establish precisely the year of the great discoverer’s death.

‘It pleased God to take him,’ says the manuscript cited above, ‘after he had governed the island ... not as its lord, but as a father and companion to all its inhabitants.’ The discoverer’s remains were buried in the Church of Conceição de Cima, now the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), which he had built as a family vault for himself and his descendants. Zargo’s tomb stood in the chancel, as was generally customary for church founders and patrons. We read elsewhere ‘that the building was arranged so that the grave ... lay in the middle of the chancel, with a stone tomb above it so high that it made the place especially venerable and imposing’. It is said that, many years later, the nuns secured the removal of the imposing mausoleum because it obstructed their view of the altar. It was perhaps then that the discoverer of Madeira’s remains were moved to the family vault of his son-in-law Martins Mendes de Vasconcelos.

We are inclined to believe that this affront – the removal of the mausoleum and the transfer of the discoverer’s remains, if it did indeed take place – occurred during the period of Philip’s rule. By then the donataries of Funchal had ceased to live on the island and their governing role had become merely honorary. It is hard to believe that they would otherwise have permitted the desecration of the grave of their illustrious ancestor, founder of the wealthy house whose benefits they enjoyed. Frutuoso’s commentator says that the sarcophagus of Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos bears an inscription in Gothic capitals, worn to the point of illegibility. A large marble slab in the adjacent floor bears the following epitaph:

Grave of Captain Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcellos, which he ordered to be made for himself and his heirs because the first grave slab placed here was removed. He was a descendant of the first Martim Mendes de Vasconcellos, who lies here and came to this island to marry Elena Gliz da Camara, daughter of João Gonsalves Zarco, its discoverer. Made in the year 1710.

This epitaph makes no reference to the discoverer’s remains, and it seems that the inscription in Gothic letters does not concern him either, according to someone who tried to decipher it and whom we consulted. Does it refer to Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos? Some have suggested that the slab came from Portugal, where it covered the grave of an ancestor of Zargo’s son-in-law. When the wooden flooring of the chancel of the church of Santa Clara was lifted in March 1919, two grave slabs were found there. Their epitaphs refer to the 2nd, 3rd and 5th captains-donatary of Funchal, as recounted on page 217 and following of volume II of this work. Nothing concerning the discoverer was found there.

blocks.text: The chapel of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), Quinta das Cruzes and, above all, the church of Santa Clara are modest but memorable monuments that eloquently recall the discoverer and the discovery of Madeira. These buildings deserve the respect and reverence that people everywhere accord to things closely associated with the lives of illustrious figures. The public authorities, especially the administrative bodies based in Funchal, have a grave duty to maintain them and, as far as possible, protect them from the ravages of time. As we have said elsewhere in this book, this is also a fitting occasion to mention the two-handed sword (*montante*) of João Gonçalves Zargo. It was always kept at the house at Cruzes, and a consistent tradition handed down through generations of the family that owned it establishes beyond doubt that it belonged to the illustrious discoverer. It has always been regarded as his, and the deep reverence shown there for this relic over the years further confirms its origin. It is an old weapon designed to be wielded with both hands, and is not particularly finely made. It certainly has no intrinsic or artistic value, but its more than five hundred years of existence give it great worth, and still greater worth comes from its having belonged to the great navigator who discovered this archipelago. It may be the sword Gonçalves Zargo wielded in Morocco during his attacks on the Moors, when he won a reputation as a brave and daring knight. This venerable relic is now in this city in the hands of a foreigner, who treasures it as it truly deserves. It should, however, belong to this city’s Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). The Council should arrange to acquire it and guard it with reverence in its archives until it can take a fitting place in the museum of art and antiquities that must one day be founded in this city (1921).

The idea of erecting a monument in this city to Madeira’s illustrious discoverer is an old one, but no serious attempt was ever made even to begin turning it into reality and thereby discharge the debt still owed to his glorious memory. In 1918 the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) commissioned a model for a statue of Zargo, to be erected on Avenida do Dr. Manuel de Arriaga, beyond the Entrada da Cidade. The model, by the distinguished Madeiran sculptor Francisco Franco, was exhibited at the Municipal Theatre (Teatro Municipal) on 2 March 1919. During the celebrations of Madeira’s Fifth Centenary, the monument’s foundation stone was laid on that avenue in a ceremony of exceptional grandeur, as already described on page 163 of this volume (1921).

Outside the city, high in the mountains overlooking all of Funchal, stands a bronze statue of João Gonçalves Zargo at Terreiro da Luta. It depicts the illustrious discoverer as the caravel under his command approached this island, then unknown. The monument, the work of the sculptor Francisco Franco, owes its existence entirely to the initiative of the former merchant and distinguished Madeiran Commander Manuel Gonçalves.

In 1806 the Madeiran poet Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos published a poem in Lisbon entitled *Zargueida*. Of this work and *Georgeida*, Inocêncio Francisco da Silva says: ‘He sought to sound the epic trumpet, but it is clear that this undertaking was far beyond his talent. In the two attempts he made in that genre, therefore, he never rose above mediocrity. Both, however, contain episodes that do his muse no discredit and can be read with pleasure.’ Of Medina e Vasconcelos’s compositions, *Zargueida* brought him the greatest renown and remains the best known of them all today. It is an epic poem in ottava rima, fashioned in the classical forms of the old epic. Divided into ten cantos, it contains more than five thousand lines. It concerns the discovery of Madeira by João Gonçalves Zargo, taking the discoverer’s surname as its title. It includes a series of interesting episodes and some successful poetic digressions, foremost among them the legend of Robert Machin. The discovery of this island is not described until canto X. The poem is preceded by a sonnet dedicated to Bocage, to which that distinguished poet replies with another sonnet, undoubtedly the finest composition in this volume (1921).

The preceding passages about Gonçalves Zargo, reproduced word for word from the first edition of this work, should be compared with the fuller account of the subject on pages 354 ff. of vol. I of the 1st edition. That account also corrects some statements made here at the time, especially the notes concerning the precise date of the discovery and the names of those who carried out this undertaking, whether by chance or design (see I-355). The further information we present below is also of particular interest to this subject.

blocks.text: The article ‘Alguns Documentos do Mosteiro de Santa Clara do Funchal’, published on pp. 171 ff. of volume IV of *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*, seeks to establish the correct spelling of the Funchal captain-donatary’s surname. It argues that it should be written Zargo, not Zarco, as it appears in many places. The article reproduces a document from 1447, including a facsimile, in which the surname is spelt Zargo. A question naturally arises: during the twenty-two years between the start of settlement and 1447, had João Gonçalves always spelt his surname with a g and never with a c? Such changes in names, family names, surnames and nicknames are not rare today, and were even more common in the past. The cited document gives grounds for a presumption that should not be dismissed altogether, but it does not establish a claim so indisputable that doubt is impermissible.

It is worth noting that Gaspar Frutuoso, author of *Saudades da Terra*, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, its distinguished commentator, and almost all the writers who have dealt with the subject used the spelling Zarco, not Zargo.

The conjectures about the probable year of João Gonçalves Zargo’s death were fully resolved by the evidence in a valuable article by the distinguished writer João Cabral do Nascimento, published in Funchal’s *Diario de Noticias* on 23 April 1927. It proves beyond doubt that he died in 1467, a valuable piece of information for Madeiran history.

The 1939 volume of the aforementioned *Arquivo Histórico* published a detailed article on João Gonçalves Zargo’s two-handed sword, discussed above. It sought to challenge the prevailing belief that the sword had belonged to the man to whom it had been attributed for centuries, but did not establish its case beyond dispute. As is well known, the public-spirited industrialist Henrique Hinton acquired the sword and gave it to the Funchal Municipal Museum, where it is held. Of particular interest on this subject is an article published in *Diário da Madeira* on 16 November 1939. Readers wishing to learn more about the matter should consult it.

The fitting tribute to João Gonçalves Zargo’s memory mentioned earlier was fully realised on 28 May 1934, when the statue erected on Avenida Arriaga was solemnly unveiled, as already described on page 394 of volume II of this *Elucidário*.

The fruit of this *Rubus*, known as bramble blackberries, is edible and has a pleasant flavour, but eating large quantities can cause colic. A decoction of the bramble’s young shoots and leaves is used as a gargle for throat ailments.

A populated locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, known then, as it still is, as Lugar. When the municipality (*concelho*) was created in 1914 and the town (*vila*) in 1928, it was also given the name Vila and became the seat of that municipality (see Ribeira Brava and the other entries under that heading).

– He was the first Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) governor to administer this archipelago. He was appointed on 15 June 1828. On the 25th of the same month, the frigate *Príncipe Real* arrived at Funchal with him aboard, but Governor and Captain-General José Lúcio Travassos Valdez prevented him from landing. As the article ‘Occupation of Madeira by Miguelite Troops’ relates, José Maria Monteiro landed after the royalist forces had taken the island and took office on 24 August 1828.

His term of office was short, but it was remembered with sorrow for his abuses of power and the indignities he inflicted on the archipelago’s inhabitants. The ominous special judicial commission (alçada) that came to the island during his rule, presided over by the high court judge (*desembargador*) Francisco António Maciel Monteiro, committed grave abuses. Its inquisitorial judicial inquiry (*devassa*) implicated a hundred people, many of whom were imprisoned and exiled from the island; a considerable number were sent to our overseas possessions. Emigration by people of every social class fleeing persecution was extensive, particularly to England, Brazil and North America. A considerable number of public officials were dismissed, and many were imprisoned and sent to Lisbon. (See Special Judicial Commissions.)

José Maria Monteiro became notorious not only for his persecution of the island’s Liberals but also for his lack of dignity and scruples. On one occasion, he even took part of the money intended to pay the troops. It is said that he often visited the homes of the *malhados* (‘piebalds’, a nickname for the Liberals) accompanied by constables (*quadrilheiros*), taking anything of value he saw. Two of his sons also distinguished themselves in these exploits. They were blamed for a major theft at the Quinta do Palheiro, the *quinta* (country estate) belonging to João de Carvalhal.

José Maria Monteiro, a naval captain who held a court appointment under Miguel I, left Madeira in late April 1830, after his successor, Dom Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo, had arrived. For his biography, see what we wrote on p. 113 of vol. I and p. 95 of vol. II, where we discussed Colonel José António de Azevedo Lemos and Joaquim Melchior Gonçalves.

blocks.text: The Spanish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) Dom Antonio Herédia was part of the army that entered Portugal under the command of the Duke of Alba in 1580. In 1602 he came to Madeira as captain of the Castilian Garrison Company. He later commanded the same garrison and subsequently governed the entire archipelago in the governor’s absence. He was the founder of the Herédia family in Madeira, whose last representatives were Francisco Correia Herédia, Antonio Correia Herédia and Francisco Correia Herédia, Viscount of Ribeira Brava (see those entries). Dom Antonio Herédia and his descendants formed ties with the most prominent Madeiran families. The important Britos entailed estate (*morgadio*) passed into the Herédia family. Its principal seat was in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, at the chantry (capela) of Nossa Senhora da Apresentação (Our Lady of the Presentation), in the locality (*sítio*) that still bears that name today. Beside it stood a large manor house, one of the largest residences outside Funchal. Both the house and the chantry were demolished long ago.

blocks.text: He lived in Funchal around the middle of the 18th century and, according to tradition, was a wealthy man. On one occasion, he invited several friends to spend the day enjoying various amusements in a cave east of the site where the lazaretto now stands. They all died when the ground above collapsed. Only one person escaped: a Black servant of Dom Cosme, who had been some distance from the cave and brought news of the terrible disaster he had witnessed back to the city.
Seafarers know the site of the disaster as the furna de D. Cosme.

From 1679 to 1684, Father Dom Zenóbio de Medicis, son of Dom Cosme de Medicis, studied at the Faculty of Theology of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). It is therefore reasonable to believe that the disaster occurred well before the middle of the 18th century, since it is unlikely that Dom Cosme de Medicis was still alive at that time.
It was founded in 1621 by the priest Jerónimo da Silva and stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior. See Monuments and Terreiro da Luta.

This distinguished woman was born in Madras, British India, on 3 October 1840. She settled in Madeira in 1880 and, two years later, opened a girls’ school at the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace). She named it St. Georges High School, and it was attended by many girls from Funchal’s leading families. After closing the school around 1892, she rebuilt the old hospital in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz using charitable donations. There she admitted a number of patients and set up a pharmacy, providing outstanding care for the sick and poor of that municipality (*concelho*). She founded a diocesan religious community whose hospital work and teaching in many schools across several parishes earned it the highest praise and the gratitude of the people of this island.

In 1907, during a smallpox epidemic, Miss Wilson took charge of the isolation hospital established at the Gonçalo Aires lazaretto. The circumstances were grave, and the most distressing consequences were feared. But her service was so remarkable that it soon dispelled the unfounded fears of many people, who were still affected by the tragic events of January 1905.

blocks.text: On this subject, one of the authors of this work wrote in the former *Heraldo da Madeira*:

‘Miss Wilson placed her boundless self-sacrifice and her great, unfailing charity at the service of those unfortunate people suffering from smallpox, without seeking the slightest advantage or the smallest reward. She thus took her place among the great benefactors of humanity who do good for its own sake, aspiring only to the approval of their own conscience and to rewards in the life beyond the grave.

‘Alongside that incomparable charity, her most kindly heart holds such reserves of tenderness, affection and gentleness that she is a veritable providence to the patients at the lazaretto, always with a smile of hope and consolation lighting her face.

‘In its ignorance and excessive credulity, skilfully exploited by those who should have been its true mentors and guides, the people imagined the lazaretto as Ugolino’s prison or the cave of Cacus. There, they believed, patients endured the worst abuses, from assaults on their modesty to the most heinous murders. All this was no more than a legend, merely the product of a vile campaign of exploitation. Yet for the general public it became an unshakeable belief, an unquestioned truth that seemed impossible to dispel or destroy.

Miss Wilson had to struggle tenaciously against these deep-rooted prejudices, superstitions and fears. The first smallpox patients entered the isolation hospital with great misgivings. Before long, however, the spell was completely broken. Those imagined horrors gradually faded, and at the lazaretto the patients found only the ardent flame of charity shining brightly in a woman’s heart.
‘Today she is there as a spirit of goodness, showering benefits in abundance, a source of brilliant light illuminating so many minds, a rainbow of peace and hope comforting troubled hearts’.

With the establishment of the new political regime, Miss Wilson had to leave Madeira. She returned to Funchal, however, and died on 18 October 1916 at the former Convent of São Bernardino (St Bernardino of Siena) in Câmara de Lobos. On 15 April 1939, her remains were moved to the chantry (capela) in the building on Rua do Carmo that houses the headquarters of the religious congregation she had founded.

As stated above, Mary Jane Wilson founded a diocesan religious congregation in 1884, naming it the Franciscan Sisters of Our Lady of Victories. It received the full approval of the ecclesiastical authorities. Devoted particularly to hospital work and the elementary education of poor children, the congregation has performed outstanding services here in Madeira, as everyone without exception acknowledges, always with the greatest zeal and dedication. Today, the institutions providing care that have been entrusted to it could not do without its beneficial work in their management. A considerable number of its members already work selflessly in the Christian missions of Portuguese Africa.

blocks.text: In several dozen articles scattered throughout this work, particularly those on pages 139 and 303 onwards of volume II and the articles cited there, we discuss this archipelago’s industries at some length. It would have been better to bring them into a closer and more logical order, but pressing circumstances prevented us from doing so.

Because it may shed light on these subjects, we should also mention the writer and economist Peres Trancoso’s pamphlet *O Trabalho Português, I, Madeira*, published in 1929. It deals with the sources of this archipelago’s economic wealth and its industrial and commercial development, although we may disagree with several statements in the work.

We wish to draw particular attention to some of the author’s conclusions. The statistical data on which they are based are unknown; those data should have been included in the work, or at least their authoritative and reliable source should have been cited.
The notes under the heading ‘Wealth’ are of interest. We reproduce them word for word:

blocks.text: With Madeira’s population at approximately 200,000, wealth per person is 6,670 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis), or £67 in round figures. This is low in relation to the island’s productive wealth and potential, and only shows that laws restricting income, excessive taxes and laws taxing exports, etc., impoverish the island and upset its natural economy. Nevertheless, the numerical conclusion is no cause for despair, for the future looks bright for the beautiful island of Madeira, until one day it takes its rightful place in the nation’s overall economy.

blocks.text: A chantry (capela) dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Fé stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho. Manuel Gonçalves Lisboa founded it in 1668, and it gave its name to the locality (*sítio*) where it was built.

At the locality of Mirante da Terra do Baptista, in the parish of Porto da Cruz, Diogo Dias de Ornelas e Vasconcellos, holder of the entail (*morgado*), founded a chantry with the same dedication. The deed of endowment was dated 25 November 1825, and the inspection required for permission to hold religious services there took place on 11 August 1826. It no longer exists.

blocks.text: During the revolt that broke out in Torres Vedras on 4 February 1844, aimed at bringing down Costa Cabral’s government, 23 insurgents were arrested and sent to Madeira. They included the lawyers António Maria Ribeiro da Costa Holtreman and Leonel Tavares Cabral, Commercial Court judge Lourenço de Oliveira Grijó, Canon Dr Manuel Joaquim Cardoso Castelo Branco and eight army officers.

Some of these political prisoners arrived aboard the brig *Douro*, which reached Funchal on 20 April, and were taken to the Ilhéu fortress (*Fortaleza do Ilhéu*). The rest came aboard the cutter *Andorinha*, which arrived here on the 28th of the same month, and were held in the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*). All were released as soon as unofficial news of the failure of the Torres Vedras revolt reached Madeira.

blocks.text: In 1919, after the monarchist revolution early that year, more political prisoners were brought to Funchal. They arrived aboard the steamship *Africa* of the Empresa Nacional de Navegação, which had been requisitioned as a troop transport. The 289 prisoners, accompanied by a naval force, disembarked on 8 May, three days after the *Africa* arrived, and were housed in the Gonçalo Aires lazaretto. Among them were the former minister João de Azevedo Coutinho, the former colonel João de Almeida, the Count of Sucena, the Count of Arrochela, the Viscount of Siqueira and João Moreira de Almeida. A force of 30 naval ratings and 1 sergeant remained in Funchal to guard the lazaretto, joined for the same purpose by an infantry detachment commanded by a second lieutenant. On the harbour master’s orders, all vessels were forbidden to pass through or remain in the stretch of sea between the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) and Cabo Garajau.

Despite these precautions, 8 prisoners, including the Count of Sucena, were found to be missing on 3 June. It later emerged that they had all reached Las Palmas aboard the motor launch *Glafiberta*, owned by the sportsman Humberto dos Passos, who had arranged the escape. On how they escaped, we read the following in a newspaper: ‘One fine afternoon, almost all the political prisoners held in the Funchal lazaretto left the building on the pretext of getting some air and gathered on the narrow strip of beach immediately below it. The guards merely watched them from the lazaretto windows. For a while they sang, romped about and cheered. When the uproar was at its height and the guards were distracted by the revelry, a boat sent from the *Glafiberta* approached the beach and took aboard the 8 prisoners without haste... Hours later, the motor launch, under tow by the *Milano* of the Blandy firm (which did not know what service had been requested of its tug), headed towards the Desertas before turning south, bound for the Canary Islands’.
The owner of the *Glafiberta* went with the eight prisoners. Days earlier, he had asked the harbour master for permission to take his boat on a voyage around the island.

Of the remaining prisoners held at the lazaretto, 7 were released following a telegram received from the Minister of War on 13 May. All the others left for Lisbon aboard various passenger steamships that called at Funchal between June and August. The steamship *Moçambique* carried the last of the 280 prisoners who had disembarked at Funchal on 8 May.
